analysis.one_liner: Expands federal housing vouchers toward every eligible low-income family and funds programs to end homelessness.
analysis.headline: Introduced August 5, 2025 by Rep. Maxine Waters with 24 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to two House committees and has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make rental assistance a guarantee for low-income families. It adds 500,000 new housing vouchers in the first year and 1,000,000 more per year through 2028, then phases in an open-ended entitlement so that any eligible low-income family can get a voucher, reaching all low-income families by 2033. It bans landlords from refusing tenants because they pay with a housing voucher or other lawful income, sends $1 billion a year in emergency grants to the areas with the worst homelessness (at least 75% required to go to permanent supportive housing under a Housing First approach), puts another $1 billion a year into the national Housing Trust Fund with priority for people who are homeless, and makes homelessness funding permanent rather than reauthorized every few years.
analysis.who_benefits: Extremely low-income renters, people experiencing homelessness or on the years-long voucher waiting lists, families facing eviction or overcrowding, people on SSI or disability benefits, and tenants who today can be turned away by landlords simply because they pay with a voucher.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Extremely low-income renters and homeless families

how_it_helps.text: Adds 500,000 incremental housing choice vouchers in fiscal 2025 and 1,000,000 more each year through 2028, targeted first to families at or below 50% of the extremely low-income limit, SSI recipients, and households experiencing homelessness, overcrowding, or eviction.

Starting in fiscal 2029, makes vouchers an entitlement that phases in by income level each year until every low-income family qualifies in 2033, converting rental assistance from a limited program with waiting lists into a guarantee.

Adds 'source of income' — including housing vouchers, Social Security and SSI benefits, child support, and savings — as a protected class under the Fair Housing Act, so landlords cannot refuse applicants for how they pay rent.

Appropriates $1 billion per year through 2029 in emergency grants to the areas with the highest need, requiring at least 75% to go to permanent supportive housing and a Housing First approach, plus $100 million per year for outreach staff — with grant money barred from law enforcement uses.
Appropriates $1 billion per year to the Housing Trust Fund for five years, requiring priority for homeless households and capping tenants' rent share at 30% of income in funded units.
Permanently authorizes McKinney-Vento homelessness grants and permanently extends the U.S. Interagency Council on Homelessness, ending the cycle of short-term reauthorizations.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a new open-ended voucher entitlement plus roughly $2 billion a year in direct appropriations while it runs. Landlords, including small ones, would have to comply with Fair Housing Act protections for voucher holders and other non-wage income. Public housing agencies would administer a far larger caseload, with new administrative fees set to cover it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; landlords face new rules

drawbacks.text: The voucher entitlement is an open-ended federal commitment: once every low-income family is covered in 2033, the annual cost would run into the tens of billions of dollars with no cap, whichever party is in power.

The bill requires priority in grant formulas and competitions for jurisdictions that adopt 15-year affordability policies and decriminalize homelessness, which draws federal money toward local policy choices some communities dispute and requires HUD to build a regulatory process to evaluate local zoning and policing.

Small landlords would face federal discrimination liability for refusing voucher holders, and the bill expands project-based voucher agreements with no percentage limit, changing how rental assistance is delivered in some markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and concrete — universal rental assistance for low-income families and a funded plan aimed at ending chronic homelessness, in a country where voucher waiting lists run for years. The cost is genuinely large too: an uncapped entitlement phased in over eight years, plus $2 billion a year in grants, with execution risk in HUD's new grant formula and local-policy criteria. The bill includes guardrails (a bar on using the money in the Moving to Work program, a 5% cap on grant administration, recapture of security-deposit funds), but its scale and permanence make it a major fiscal commitment that would be hard to scale back later.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in August 2025 and sent to the Financial Services and Judiciary Committees, and neither has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters, the ranking Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, introduced the Ending Homelessness Act of 2025 on August 5, 2025.
Twenty-four House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The bill was referred to both the Financial Services Committee and the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction.
No markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor action has been scheduled or taken since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No new program exists, so the status quo holds: the federal government keeps paying vouchers only for the families already served, tenants stay on waiting lists, and landlords face no new obligation to accept voucher holders or other non-wage income.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Voucher landlords and the status quo

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ending Homelessness Act of 2025, a rewritten version of her long-running voucher-expansion bill.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; all 24 are Democrats and none are Republicans.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors are Democrats and the sponsor is a House Democratic leader; no Republican has joined, and the bill has seen no action since its August 2025 referral.

industries.note: The bill makes vouchers the permanent channel for federal rental aid, with payments flowing to private landlords who own the units tenants rent — a large, guaranteed stream of rent-paying customers. In exchange, landlords lose the ability to refuse applicants because they pay with a voucher, SSI, or child support, which is exactly the practice the Fair Housing Act change targets.

industries.industry: Nonprofit and faith-based housing and homeless-services providers
industries.note: Roughly $2 billion a year in McKinney-Vento emergency, outreach, and Housing Trust Fund money would flow to nonprofits (including faith-based organizations, which the bill explicitly protects from eligibility discrimination), funding permanent supportive housing construction and outreach staff.

The Housing Trust Fund money and the permanent supportive housing requirement (at least 75% of emergency grants) create a funded pipeline of new affordable units, with priority occupancy for people experiencing homelessness and a 30%-of-income rent cap for tenants.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to committee in the first year of a Congress that receive no markup or hearing by late in the session rarely reach the floor. With a purely Democratic sponsor base and two committee jurisdictions, the realistic path this Congress is narrow: the provisions could be folded into a larger housing or appropriations package, but as a standalone bill it is very unlikely to get a vote.
